description: We are 3 grade 11 students from Toronto participating in the NASA space apps challenge.
summary: Over the past 48 hours, we have developed a dashboard capable of interpreting custom user scenarios or presets and synthesizing data from verified NASA sources, namely the PSI repository and SAFFIRE, to provide a deep analysis of flame behaviour. What initially seemed like endless tables/pages of aerospace jargon is now presented as a comprehensive summary of research that correlates precisely with fire safety requirements for crew, facilitating habitability. In addition, EMBER can successfully identify and pull on data that aids in the modelling of scenarios and flammability in space, as well as highlighting pioneering research in the development of next-gen fire safety equipment. Potential ground (Earth) applications for evidence concluded from research are also provided by EMBER. Finally, if the user has any uncertainties or doubts about the data provided, we have anticipated some common queries that they can delve into. For questions outside our scope of prediction, the Google Gemini-powered query bar is at their disposal.
details:
Traditional research tools and the PSI repository organize much of this information by individual study, so comparing results across tables takes a painstaking amount of time. EMBER brings the consulted data, findings, source links and data-quality issues together, making evidence easier to explore while keeping its limits visible.

How it works: EMBER organizes NASA’s fire research into a shared, traceable dataset. Users describe a habitat scenario, and EMBER matches it to relevant experiments, presents measured findings and identifies gaps; its AI answers are thoroughly checked against the cited sources.

Findings: This tab presents eight results calculated from NASA’s measurements, such as how smoke particles grow as smoke ages. Each finding shows the source rows behind it and explains the method and limitations.

Analyze: Users can compare two scenarios for one fuel to see which NASA tests apply, what evidence gaps remain and what new tests could help address them. They can save scenarios as comparison baselines and reproduce the analysis.

Data: This tab brings the research data we consulted into one shared atlas, with links back to its source rows and cells, and documents problems found in the source files. Putting the data in one consistent structure makes it easier to compare studies across investigations and tables.

How We Know: This tab explains EMBER’s AI grounding, data verification checks, and assessment of accuracy and credibility. These checks support traceability and transparency, which are essential when presenting evidence related to fire safety.

Tools and development: EMBER was built with TypeScript and JavaScript using React, and runs on Node.js with Vercel Functions; it is hosted on Vercel. Google Gemini powers the question-and-answer feature. We also used Claude to help with programming, reviewed its contributions before accepting them, and marked its contributions with co-author tags in the Git repository.
